sources.citation: Philip JH. Workbook for Gas Man(R): a simulation and teaching tool. Chestnut Hill, MA: Med Man Simulations, Inc.; document dated 2012-05-16, preface dated October 2010. Appendix B, 'The Gas Man Approach', Model Parameters table (Table A-1), page 168, and Appendix C, 'Gas Man System Defaults', pages 171-172.
sources.note: Tier 3, reference implementation, CITED AND NOT ADOPTED - the only entry in any of this project's data files where the Workbook is cited and the value taken from it is not the value stored (see docs/MODEL.md, 'Source hierarchy'). READ AT THE SOURCE 2026-09-06, from a copy of the front matter and appendices supplied by the project owner, and RE-READ 2026-09-15 from the private reference corpus (stuthedew/open-anesthesia-sim-references), which now holds the whole document; this repository still does not hold it, because it is publisher-copyright material and the repository is public. The title cited above was 'Gas Man(R) Workbook and Laboratory Manual' until 2026-09-15 and is now the one on the document's title page; data/patients/reference_adult.json carries why. Page 168's Model Parameters table gives, under Volume / Flow / Rel. Flow: Circuit 8.0; Alveoli 2.5; Blood 5.00; VRG 6.0, 3.80, 0.76; Muscle 33.0, 0.90, 0.18; Fat 14.5, 0.30, 0.06. SO THE PUBLISHED CIRCUIT VOLUME IS 8.0 L AND THIS FILE STORES 6.0 L. That is a deliberate departure and not a transcription error: the project owner ruled on 2026-09-01 that which value is used is not critical here, and 6.0 was already the shipped figure. It is recorded so that a later reader finds a decision rather than an accident, which is the whole reason this file exists (PL-4YY1). WHAT THE DEPARTURE IS WORTH, SINCE THE READER SHOULD NOT HAVE TO WORK IT OUT. The circuit's fresh-gas wash-in time constant is tau_C = V_C / VdotF, so at this file's 4.0 L/min it is 90 s here against 120 s at the published 8.0 L - a 25 percent shorter machine lag. That lag is the part of the early rise in inspired concentration that belongs to the apparatus rather than to uptake, which is the single most-taught point about a circle system, so the difference is visible on the curve even though it changes nothing about the patient. A run reproducing a published Gas Man trajectory must set 8.0 L rather than assume it. THE TABLE SUPPLIES NO FRESH GAS FLOW AT ALL, AND NEITHER DOES THE PROGRAM'S OWN DEFAULTS FILE. Its Circuit row carries a volume and no entry in the Flow column, and the interface defaults described at page 183 ('Patient default options include:', Appendix E) are qualitative and carry no numbers. Appendix C, 'Gas Man System Defaults', pages 171-172, prints GASMAN.INI verbatim and was read 2026-09-15: its [Volumes] block gives CKT=8.0, which is the same published circuit volume as the table and confirms the 8.0 figure this file departs from without needing De Wolf et al.; its [Defaults] block gives VA=4, CO=5, a default agent and a default circuit mode AND NO FRESH GAS FLOW. So the absence is now checked against the program's stored defaults rather than only against a qualitative description of its controls, and default_fresh_gas_flow_l_min still has no counterpart in this source and none in any other this project has reached; the provenance_gap below says so rather than leaving the silence to be read as an oversight.

sources.citation: De Wolf AM, Van Zundert TC, De Cooman S, Hendrickx JF. Theoretical effect of hyperventilation on speed of recovery and risk of rehypnotization following recovery - a Gas Man simulation. BMC Anesthesiology. 2012;12:22. DOI 10.1186/1471-2253-12-22. Methods.
sources.note: Tier 3, reference implementation, cited and not adopted. READ AT FULL TEXT 2026-09-13 from PubMed Central (PMC3502091). Its Methods state the settings held constant across every simulation in that study: 'a 70 kg patient, an anesthesia breathing circuit volume of 8 L, a FGF of 1 L.min-1, an alveolar minute ventilation (VA) of 5 L.min-1, a functional residual capacity (FRC) of 2.5 L, and a cardiac output (Q) of 5 L.min-1'. IT IS HERE AS THE REACHABLE CONFIRMATION OF THE 8 L FIGURE, AND FOR NOTHING ELSE. The Workbook entry above is the primary statement of Gas Man's circuit volume and it cannot be opened from a URL; this paper prints the same 8 L and is open access, so a reader can check that this file's departure is from 8 and not from something else. Two tier-3 documents agreeing is not evidence that either descends from a measurement. ITS FGF OF 1 L/min IS NOT A GAS MAN DEFAULT AND IS NOT EVIDENCE ABOUT THE VALUE STORED HERE. It is the operating point that study chose, stated as such, alongside an alveolar ventilation of 5 L/min that this project also does not use (the reference patient stores 4.0). Reading a study's chosen settings as a parameter set's defaults is the error this note exists to forestall.

sources.citation: Targ AG, Yasuda N, Eger EI II. Solubility of I-653, sevoflurane, isoflurane, and halothane in plastics and rubber composing a conventional anesthetic circuit. Anesthesia & Analgesia. 1989;69(2):218-225. Methods.
sources.note: Tier 1, primary measurement, CITED AND NOT ADOPTED. THE ONLY MEASURED CONVENTIONAL CIRCLE-SYSTEM VOLUME THIS PROJECT HOLDS. Read at full text 2026-09-13 from the private reference corpus (stuthedew/open-anesthesia-sim-references, supplied by the project owner); the quoted sentence and the component list below were read off the Methods directly, and the citation, author list, journal, volume, issue and pages were verified against PubMed metadata (PMID 2764290) the same day. Its Methods state, in these words: 'The total volume of the system, as measured by water filling, was 9860 ml'. WHAT THAT 9.86 L CONTAINED, WHICH IS THE WHOLE OF WHY IT IS NOT ADOPTED. The Methods list the system as three corrugated polyethylene tubes (Marquest), a polypropylene Y-piece and elbow (Marquest), a soda lime absorber including inspiratory and expiratory valves (Ohio Medical Products), fresh 15-percent-water soda lime (Dewey and Almy Sodasorb), a rubber bellows (Ohmeda) in an Air-Shields Ventimeter ventilator - and a latex reservoir bag (Marquest) attached at the Y-piece elbow TO SIMULATE THE PATIENT'S LUNGS. This file's circuit_volume_l is the apparatus alone, with the patient modelled separately in data/patients/reference_adult.json, so adopting 9.86 L would count a lung twice: once inside the circuit and again as the 2.5 L alveolar compartment. SUBTRACTING THE BAG IS NOT AVAILABLE, AND A READER WILL TRY IT, SO THE REASON IS RECORDED HERE. The paper states no bag volume, so any subtraction is a guess - and the method makes the guess worse rather than better. The volume was obtained BY WATER FILLING, and a latex reservoir bag full of water distends well past the nominal capacity it carries as a gas reservoir, by an amount depending on the static head it sat under, which is not reported. So the bag's share of 9.86 L is not its label, is not recoverable from anything published, and the apparatus-alone figure cannot be extracted from this measurement at all. A SECOND REASON THE FIGURE RUNS HIGH, STATED BECAUSE IT IS NOT OBVIOUS. The paper does not say whether the absorber held soda lime when the water filling was done, and water filling a canister of fresh soda lime would ordinarily be precluded by the fact that soda lime reacts with water. If the canister was measured empty, 9.86 L includes space the granules occupy in use, and the working GAS volume of the same circuit is smaller again. This is not resolved here and does not need to be: every unresolved direction points the same way, which is why the only claim made below is a bound. WHAT IT DOES ESTABLISH IS AN UPPER BOUND, MEASURED RATHER THAN ADOPTED. A real conventional circle system's apparatus gas volume is at most 9.86 L, on the one measurement in evidence. That bound sits above the Workbook's published 8.0 L, which sits above this file's stored 6.0 L: three figures in one order, only one of them measured, and none measuring quite the same thing - the other two are apparatus alone, this one is apparatus plus a simulated lung. THE LIKE-FOR-LIKE COMPARISON IS CLOSER THAN 6.0 AGAINST 9.86, AND IS THE ONE TO READ. What Targ measured is apparatus plus lung. This model's corresponding total is circuit_volume_l plus the reference patient's alveolar_gas_volume_l, 6.0 + 2.5 = 8.5 L, against the measured 9.86 L - 13.8 percent below, where the bare 6.0 against 9.86 reads as 39 percent below. The paper supports the comparison being made in that form: its Figures 3 and 5 draw the ideal washin and washout as 100[1 - exp(-(V/Vs)t)] with Vs = 9.86 L, so the study's own time constant is total system volume over inflow, the same tau = V/VdotF this file's other entries use. The comparison is still not an adoption - a latex bag is not a lung and this apparatus had no patient taking up agent - but a reader weighing whether 6.0 L is far from reality should weigh 8.5 against 9.86 rather than 6.0 against 9.86. WHAT THE SPREAD IS WORTH ON THE CURVE. tau_C = V_C / VdotF, so at this file's 4.0 L/min it is 90 s at the stored 6.0 L, 120 s at the published 8.0 L and 148 s at the measured 9.86 L. That lag is the part of the early rise in inspired concentration belonging to the apparatus rather than to uptake, so the spread is visible to a learner even though it changes nothing about the patient. NO STORED VALUE CHANGES, AND THAT IS NOT THIS ENTRY'S CALL TO MAKE. The project owner ruled on 2026-09-01 that which circuit volume is used is not critical here, and this measurement does not disturb that ruling: it cannot supply an apparatus-alone figure to move to. What it changes is the state of the evidence, which the provenance_gap below used to describe as unsought. ONE CAUTION ON GENERALITY. This is one circuit assembled for one study, not a clinical standard. Circle-system volume varies with tubing length, absorber size and bellows, so a measurement of a different system would land elsewhere and would not contradict this one. THE SAME PAPER IS READ FOR TWO OTHER PURPOSES, BOTH RECORDED ELSEWHERE. Its Table 1 component partition coefficients are docs/MODEL.md's 'Known limitations' entry on the model's inert circuit walls (PL-LS3H); its washin and washout comparison against the ideal exponential is what strikes circuit-wall absorption as a candidate for desflurane's elimination residual (PL-XWCY). Recorded here for PL-QBKQ.

provenance_gap: NO SOURCE IS ADOPTED FOR EITHER VALUE IN THIS FILE, AND THAT IS THE POINT OF WRITING IT DOWN. Both were hardcoded as dataclass field defaults in src/anesthesia_sim/core/circuit.py until 2026-09-13, where tools/doc_check.py's check_provenance could not see them: that check walks data files in both directions, so a scientific constant that never entered one was structurally invisible to the only tool built to catch a missing citation. PL-4YY1 moved them here for that reason, and changed neither. circuit_volume_l = 6.0 departs deliberately from the Workbook's published 8.0, on the project owner's ruling of 2026-09-01 that which value is used is not critical; the Workbook entry above carries the figure, the decision and what the 25 percent shorter machine lag looks like on the curve. default_fresh_gas_flow_l_min = 4.0 has no published counterpart at all. The Workbook's parameter table gives the circuit no flow entry, its interface defaults are described without numbers, and the two Gas Man simulation studies this project has read chose their own flows for their own purposes (De Wolf et al. 1 L/min; Meybohm et al. 10 L/min for washout). It is a teaching default, not a clinical recommendation (project owner, 2026-09-20, ratified, over lowering the default to match contemporary low-flow practice; PL-NM7X). What it is chosen for is legibility, not representativeness: it sits well inside the supported interval core/supported_ranges.py declares (0.0 to 10.0 L/min) and puts the circuit time constant at 90 s - long enough that a learner sees the machine lag as a distinct phase of the early rise, short enough that it resolves inside the first few minutes of a teaching run. At 0.5 L/min that same lag is about 12 minutes, which is longer than the demonstration it exists to make. That is a design rationale and not a measurement, and it is labelled as one here. UNTIL 2026-09-20 THIS SENTENCE ALSO CALLED 4.0 'a routine mid-range clinical fresh gas flow'. That was a claim about clinical practice, it was never sourced, and it is withdrawn rather than re-sourced; the paragraph below is what replaced it. WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS GAP, AND WHAT ONE MEASUREMENT HAS SINCE CHANGED ABOUT IT (PL-QBKQ, 2026-09-13). The gap wants two things: a published circle-system internal volume measured on real apparatus, and a stated clinical convention for a default flow. THE FIRST HAS NOW BEEN SOUGHT AND PARTLY FOUND, AND THIS FILE NO LONGER SAYS OTHERWISE. Targ, Yasuda and Eger 1989 - the entry above - measured a conventional circle system at 9860 ml by water filling. It does not close the gap, because that figure includes a latex reservoir bag standing in for the patient's lungs and the apparatus's own share cannot be recovered from it; the entry gives the reasoning in full. What it supplies instead is a measured UPPER BOUND of 9.86 L, which leaves the stored 6.0 L and the Workbook's published 8.0 L both admissible and orders the three. So the honest statement of the gap is now narrower than 'unsought': what is missing is a published apparatus-alone volume, measured without a lung attached or with the lung's volume stated separately, and no such measurement has been found. THE SECOND HAS NOW BEEN SOUGHT, AND NO SOURCE STATES ONE (PL-4DCG's machine survey 2026-09-19, confirmed for PL-NM7X 2026-09-20). No surveyed machine publishes a startup fresh gas flow; docs/machine-survey.md section (a2) records the search and what it returned. So default_fresh_gas_flow_l_min = 4.0 still has no published counterpart, and the honest statement of this half of the gap is now narrower than 'not sought': what is missing is not a source nobody looked for, but a published startup convention that does not appear to exist. WHAT THE LITERATURE CARRIES IS A RECOMMENDATION, NOT A MEASUREMENT OF PRACTICE, AND THAT DIFFERENCE IS WHY 4.0 IS LABELLED ABOVE RATHER THAN DEFENDED. Kalmar et al. conclude that 'routine clinical practice using what historically is called "low flow anaesthesia" (e.g. 2 L/min FGF) should be abandoned' in favour of automated minimal-flow delivery (J Clin Monit Comput 2022;36(6):1601-1610, PMID 34978655, DOI 10.1007/s10877-021-00803-z). READ AT FULL TEXT 2026-09-20 from PubMed Central (PMC9637609): the quoted sentence is the abstract's closing one, and the body's Conclusion states it again without the parenthesised figure. It is a normative recommendation drawn from a single-centre retrospective of 25 cases per group on one workstation, not a survey of what flows are used. What it does establish about practice is its own comparator - a fixed 2 L/min group the paper calls conventional low flow, which already sits below this file's 4.0. TWO PAPERS CITED BESIDE IT DO NOT SUPPORT A CLAIM ABOUT PRACTICE AT ALL, AND THAT IS RECORDED HERE SO A LATER READER DOES NOT RE-DERIVE IT. Candries et al. randomised 0.2 to 6 L/min in 28 patients as the protocol of a Gas Man validation study (J Clin Monit Comput 2022;36(6):1881-1890, PMID 35318567, DOI 10.1007/s10877-022-00842-0), and Hoffmann et al. ran 0.3, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 L/min in vitro into a 2 L test lung and describe those settings as reflecting clinical conditions (Anesthesiology 2025;142(6):1038-1046, PMID 40073301, DOI 10.1097/ALN.0000000000005445). Both were ABSTRACT READ 2026-09-20 from PubMed; neither has a PubMed Central full text, and a 2026-09-20 check of the private reference corpus (stuthedew/open-anesthesia-sim-references) found neither in it. Neither claim above needs a methods section, because both flow ranges are stated in full in the abstracts. A STUDY'S CHOSEN FLOW RANGE IS NOT A REPORT OF PRACTICE - the same error the De Wolf entry above forestalls for its 1 L/min - and Hoffmann's range contains 4, 5 and 6 L/min, so reading it as evidence that the field has moved below 4 L/min gets it backwards. NEITHER GAP IS REQUIRED for a value the owner has ruled non-critical. THE DELIVERABLE FRESH GAS FLOW RANGE IS NULL, AND THE NULL IS THE RECORD RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT (PL-8PS6, 2026-09-20). deliverable_fresh_gas_flow_range says what this machine's flowmeters can physically set. It is null here because no such figure was reachable: docs/machine-survey.md section (b8), 'Flow bounds, minimum oxygen flow, and the hypoxic guard', reports that no minimum oxygen flow, minimum total flow or deliverable range was found for ANY of the eight machines surveyed on 2026-09-19. The governing standard it names is ISO 80601-2-13:2022, Medical electrical equipment - Part 2-13: Particular requirements for basic safety and essential performance of an anaesthetic workstation, second edition 2022-04, amended by ISO 80601-2-13:2022/Amd 1:2026; ITS TEXT WAS NOT REACHED AND NO CLAIM ABOUT WHAT IT REQUIRES IS MADE HERE, by this file or by the survey. The standard is named as a pointer for a session that can open it, not as a citation. WHAT NULL MEANS TO THE CODE, WHICH IS NOT 'UNLIMITED'. A null range is an absence of claim: core/supported_ranges.py's 0.0 to 10.0 L/min envelope is then the only bound on the flow, which is exactly the behaviour this file shipped before the field existed, so nothing displayed or refused changes. It is emphatically not a statement that this breathing system will deliver any flow whatever. A profile that DOES declare a range narrows what the circuit accepts and cannot widen the envelope, because BreathingCircuit checks both claims and each refuses in its own words. WHY THE OTHER TWO SLOTS SECTION (b8) NAMES ARE NOT FIELDS HERE. docs/machine-abstraction.md's field table lists minimum_total_flow_l_min and minimum_oxygen_flow_l_min beside the range. Neither is added by this item, on the abstraction's own admission rule that a field exists only if something consumes it. A minimum total fresh gas flow IS the deliverable range's own floor, and storing it twice would put two names on one number in a safety-critical file; a minimum oxygen flow reaches nothing this model computes, because the model carries one volatile agent and no oxygen at all. The second becomes admissible the day a hypoxic guard needs it, which is a model extension rather than a data question.
